chapter.name: Waves
chapter.blurb: The chapter introduces mechanical waves, transverse and longitudinal, and describes a sinusoidal travelling wave by y = a sin(kx - omega t + phi) with its amplitude, phase, wavelength, period and frequency. It obtains the wave speed v = lambda nu, the speed sqrt(T/mu) on a stretched string and the speed of sound in solids, liquids and gases including Newton's formula and Laplace's correction. It then treats superposition and interference, reflection, stationary waves and the normal modes of strings and pipes, and ends with beats.

scope_in.item: Explain that a wave is a pattern of disturbance that moves through a medium without the medium as a whole moving, that it transports energy and carries information, and distinguish mechanical waves (need a medium, depend on its elastic properties) from electromagnetic waves (no medium, all with speed c in vacuum)

Explain how elastic coupling (a chain of springs, bogies of a train, compressions and rarefactions in air, atoms in a lattice) lets a disturbance travel while each part only oscillates about its place; distinguish a wind from a sound wave

Define transverse and longitudinal waves, and say which media support each (shear modulus for transverse waves, so not fluids; longitudinal waves in solids, liquids and gases); water waves (capillary and gravity) as a combination of both (Example 14.1)

Use the progressive-wave displacement y = a sin(kx - omega t + phi): amplitude, phase and initial phase angle, direction of travel (+x or -x), a sin + b cos combined into one sine with a = sqrt(A^2 + B^2) and phi = tan^-1(B/A), the longitudinal form s(x, t) (Example 14.2)
Use wavelength lambda = 2 pi/k, angular wave number k (rad/m), period T = 2 pi/omega, frequency nu = 1/T = omega/2 pi, angular frequency omega
Use the wave speed v = omega/k = lambda nu = lambda/T for any progressive wave, and the fact that the medium fixes the speed while the source fixes the frequency
Use the speed of a transverse wave on a stretched string v = sqrt(T/mu), mu = m/L, including its dimensional-analysis origin (Example 14.3)
Use the speed of longitudinal waves: v = sqrt(B/rho) in a fluid, v = sqrt(Y/rho) in a solid bar, Table 14.1, why solids and liquids carry sound faster than gases

Apply Newton's formula v = sqrt(P/rho) (isothermal, B = P) and Laplace's correction v = sqrt(gamma P/rho) (adiabatic, B = gamma P, gamma = 7/5 for air) to the speed of sound in an ideal gas (Example 14.4)
State and use the principle of superposition for pulses and harmonic waves, y = sum of f_i(x - vt); pulses retain their identities after crossing
Interference of two equal-amplitude harmonic waves differing in phase by phi: resultant amplitude 2a cos(phi/2), constructive (phi = 0 or a multiple of 2 pi) and destructive (phi = pi) interference
Reflection of pulses and waves: phase change of pi at a rigid boundary, none at a non-rigid (open or free) boundary, echo; partial reflection and transmission at an interface of two media

Stationary waves from two identical waves in opposite directions: y = 2a sin kx cos omega t, nodes at x = n lambda/2, antinodes at x = (n + 1/2) lambda/2, spacing lambda/2, same frequency for every element

Normal modes: a string fixed at both ends (nu_n = n v/2L), an air column closed at one end (odd harmonics (n + 1/2) v/2L, fundamental v/4L), and a pipe open at both ends (all harmonics); fundamental and harmonics; resonance (Example 14.5)
Beats: the resultant s = [2a cos(omega_b t)] cos(omega_a t) of two close frequencies, waxing and waning of intensity, nu_beat = nu1 - nu2, tuning by beats (Example 14.6)

concepts.name: Mechanical waves: transverse and longitudinal waves
concepts.description: What a wave is, how mechanical waves differ from electromagnetic waves, why a medium with elastic coupling can carry a disturbance, and the difference between transverse and longitudinal waves including which media support each.
concepts.idea: A wave is a pattern of disturbance that moves through a medium without the medium as a whole moving; it transports energy and information. Mechanical waves need a material medium whose elastic properties let each part act on its neighbour.
concepts.rule: In a transverse wave the particles oscillate perpendicular to the direction of propagation; in a longitudinal wave they oscillate along it. A transverse wave puts each element under shearing strain, so it needs a medium that can sustain shearing stress (solids, not fluids); a longitudinal wave needs only compressive strain, so it travels in solids, liquids and gases. Steel carries both, air only longitudinal waves. Transverse and longitudinal waves generally travel at different speeds in the same medium. Electromagnetic waves need no medium; in vacuum all have the same speed c = 299 792 458 m/s. Wind (air moving as a whole) is not a sound wave (a disturbance of pressure and density).
concepts.example: Sound from a tuning fork reaches a listener: layers of air are alternately compressed and rarefied along the direction in which the sound travels, so it is a longitudinal wave, yet no air flows from the fork to the listener.

questions.q: A collection of springs is joined end to end and the spring at one end is pulled suddenly and released. Explain how a disturbance then reaches the far end although no spring moves far from its equilibrium position.
questions.a: The first spring is stretched or compressed from its equilibrium length. The second spring is joined to it, so it is stretched or compressed too, and so on along the chain. Each spring only makes small oscillations about its own equilibrium position, but the disturbance is handed on from spring to spring until it reaches the other end.
s: Each spring disturbs the next because they are joined (elastic coupling)
Each spring only oscillates about its own equilibrium position; it is the disturbance that travels to the far end

questions.q: Waves on the surface of water are of two kinds. For each kind state the typical range of wavelength and the restoring force that produces it, and explain why the particle motion in such waves makes them neither purely transverse nor purely longitudinal.
questions.a: Capillary waves are ripples of short wavelength, not more than a few centimetres, and their restoring force is the surface tension of water. Gravity waves have wavelengths from several metres to several hundred metres, and their restoring force is the pull of gravity, which tends to keep the water surface at its lowest level. In both, the particles do not just move up and down: they also move back and forth, so the motion combines transverse and longitudinal parts.
s: Capillary waves: wavelength at most a few centimetres, restoring force surface tension
Gravity waves: wavelength several metres to several hundred metres, restoring force gravity
Particles move both up and down and back and forth, so the wave is a combination of both types

questions.a: The statement is incorrect. A wind is the motion of air as a whole from one place to another. A sound wave is the propagation of a disturbance in pressure and density (compressions and rarefactions) through air: each layer of air only oscillates about its place and no air flows from the speaker to the listener.
s: Judgement: incorrect, because a sound wave does not carry the air along as a wind does

The medium is the line of people. Each person only moves a little about his or her own place; nobody walks along the line. What is carried along the line is energy (and the information that a push was given), not the people.
s: A valid situation with the medium named
Each part of the medium only oscillates about its own position (it is not carried along)
States that energy (and the pattern of disturbance, i.e. information) is transported

concepts.name: Displacement relation of a progressive wave: amplitude, phase, wavelength, period and frequency
concepts.description: The sinusoidal travelling wave y = a sin(kx - omega t + phi): meaning of amplitude, phase and initial phase angle, angular wave number and wavelength, angular frequency, period and frequency, and the direction of travel.
concepts.idea: A sinusoidal travelling wave is described by a displacement function of both position and time, fixed by an amplitude, an angular wave number, an angular frequency and an initial phase.
concepts.rule: y(x, t) = a sin(kx - omega t + phi) travels in +x; y = a sin(kx + omega t + phi) travels in -x. a is the (positive) amplitude; (kx - omega t + phi) is the phase and phi the initial phase angle, which can be made zero by choosing origin and initial time. lambda = 2 pi/k (k in rad/m), T = 2 pi/omega, nu = 1/T = omega/2 pi. At a fixed instant y is a sine function of x; at a fixed location the element executes SHM. A sin(kx - omega t) + B cos(kx - omega t) = a sin(kx - omega t + phi) with a = sqrt(A^2 + B^2) and phi = tan^-1(B/A). For a longitudinal wave s(x, t) = a sin(kx - omega t + phi), s being displacement along the direction of propagation.
concepts.example: For y = 0.08 sin(6 pi x - 30 pi t) in SI units: amplitude 0.08 m, wavelength 2 pi/(6 pi) = 1/3 m, period 2 pi/(30 pi) = 1/15 s and frequency 15 Hz.

The displacement y is a function of both the position x and the time t

questions.q: A wave on a string is y(x, t) = 0.04 sin(10 pi x - 4 pi t), with x and y in metres and t in seconds. Find its wavelength and its period.
questions.a: Comparing with y = a sin(kx - omega t): k = 10 pi rad/m and omega = 4 pi rad/s. Wavelength = 2 pi/k = 2 pi/(10 pi) = 0.2 m. Period T = 2 pi/omega = 2 pi/(4 pi) = 0.5 s.

Period = 2 pi/omega = 0.5 s

questions.q: A transverse wave on a string is y = 5 sin(kx - omega t) + 12 cos(kx - omega t), with y in cm. Write it in the form a sin(kx - omega t + phi), using a cos phi = 5 and a sin phi = 12. Find a, find tan phi, and state the largest displacement any element of the string reaches.
questions.a: Here A = 5 and B = 12. a = sqrt(A^2 + B^2) = sqrt(25 + 144) = 13 cm. tan phi = B/A = 12/5 = 2.4, so phi = tan^-1(2.4). Thus y = 13 sin(kx - omega t + phi) cm, and the largest displacement of any element equals the amplitude, 13 cm.
s: tan phi = 12/5 = 2.4
Largest displacement = amplitude = 13 cm

questions.q: (I) The phase constant phi in y = a sin(kx - omega t + phi) can always be made zero, without loss of generality, by a suitable choice of the origin on the x-axis and of the initial time. (II) At a fixed position, the constituent of the medium executes simple harmonic motion as the wave passes. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Both I and II

questions.q: Explain how the single equation y = a sin(kx - omega t) describes both the shape of the wave at one instant and the motion of one element of the medium over time.
questions.a: At a fixed instant t0 the argument is kx + constant, so y is a sine function of x: this is the shape of the wave in space. At a fixed location x0 the argument is a constant minus omega t, so y varies sinusoidally with time: this is the simple harmonic motion of the element at that location.
s: Fixed instant: y is a sine function of x, giving the shape of the wave in space
Fixed location: y varies sinusoidally with time, i.e. the element executes SHM

questions.q: Explain, by following a point of constant phase, why y = a sin(kx - omega t + phi) represents a wave travelling in the +x direction while y = a sin(kx + omega t + phi) represents one travelling in the -x direction.
questions.a: A point of fixed phase on the wave pattern satisfies kx - omega t + phi = constant. As t increases, omega t increases, so x must increase to keep kx - omega t constant: the pattern moves toward +x. For y = a sin(kx + omega t + phi) the condition is kx + omega t + phi = constant; as t increases, x must decrease to keep it constant, so the pattern moves toward -x.
s: Follows a point of constant phase: kx - omega t + phi = constant
As t increases x must increase, so the wave moves in +x
For kx + omega t the constant-phase point has x decreasing, so the wave moves in -x

questions.q: A student says: 'In y = a sin(kx - omega t) the amplitude a is taken positive, so the displacement y of the medium is always positive.' Evaluate this statement.
questions.a: The statement is incorrect. The amplitude a is the positive maximum displacement, but the sine function varies between +1 and -1, so y varies between +a and -a and is negative for part of every cycle.
s: Judgement: incorrect; a is positive but y is not
Because the sine takes values from -1 to +1, y varies between -a and +a

questions.q: Write down, in SI units, the displacement equation of a transverse wave of your own with amplitude 2 mm, wavelength 0.5 m and period 0.02 s, travelling in the -x direction with phi = 0. Give the values of k and omega that you use.
questions.a: k = 2 pi/lambda = 2 pi/0.5 = 4 pi rad/m. omega = 2 pi/T = 2 pi/0.02 = 100 pi rad/s. Because the wave travels in the -x direction the signs of kx and omega t are the same: y(x, t) = 0.002 sin(4 pi x + 100 pi t), with y and x in metres and t in seconds.
s: k = 4 pi rad/m
omega = 100 pi rad/s
y = 0.002 sin(4 pi x + 100 pi t), with the plus sign for travel in -x

concepts.name: Speed of a travelling wave and the speed of a transverse wave on a stretched string
concepts.description: The relation v = omega/k = lambda nu for any progressive wave, why the medium fixes the speed while the source fixes the frequency, and the speed sqrt(T/mu) of transverse waves on a stretched string.
concepts.idea: The speed of a mechanical wave is fixed by the elastic and inertial properties of the medium; the source fixes the frequency, and the wavelength then follows.
concepts.rule: A point of fixed phase (kx - omega t = constant) moves with speed v = omega/k = lambda nu = lambda/T: in one period the pattern advances one wavelength. lambda = v/nu. For transverse waves on a stretched string, v = sqrt(T/mu), where T is the tension (restoring force) and mu = m/L the linear mass density (inertia); this was got by dimensional analysis, v = C sqrt(T/mu), with the exact derivation giving C = 1. The speed does not depend on the wavelength or frequency of the wave.
concepts.example: A rope of mass 2.0 kg and length 5.0 m is held under a tension of 250 N: mu = 0.4 kg/m and v = sqrt(250/0.4) = sqrt(625) = 25 m/s.

Wavelength = v/nu = 22/55 = 0.4 m

questions.q: A harmonic wave of frequency 120 Hz travels at 60 m/s along a string of linear mass density 0.05 kg/m. Find (a) the tension in the string, (b) the wavelength of the wave, and (c) the tension needed to make the speed 90 m/s, the linear mass density remaining the same.
questions.a: (a) From v = sqrt(T/mu), T = mu v^2 = 0.05 x 60^2 = 180 N. (b) Wavelength = v/nu = 60/120 = 0.5 m. (c) T' = mu v'^2 = 0.05 x 90^2 = 405 N.
s: Tension T = mu v^2 = 180 N
Wavelength = v/nu = 0.5 m
New tension = 0.05 x 90^2 = 405 N

questions.q: Using the idea that the speed of a mechanical wave is set by the restoring force and the inertia of the medium, explain how the speed of a transverse wave on a string should change (a) when the tension is increased and (b) when the string is replaced by a thicker one of the same material under the same tension.
questions.a: On a string the restoring force is provided by the tension, so a larger tension makes the wave faster (v = sqrt(T/mu) increases with T). The inertial property is the linear mass density mu; a thicker string of the same material has a larger mu, which makes the wave slower, since v decreases as mu increases.
s: (a) Larger tension (restoring force) gives a larger speed
(b) Thicker string has larger mass per unit length (inertia), which gives a smaller speed

questions.q: The speed of transverse waves on a string was obtained from dimensional analysis. Show that T/mu has the dimensions of the square of a speed, and explain what the dimensional analysis can and cannot tell us about the formula.
questions.a: The dimension of mu is [M L^-1] and that of T is that of a force, [M L T^-2]. Then T/mu = [M L T^-2]/[M L^-1] = [L^2 T^-2], the dimension of speed squared, so v is proportional to sqrt(T/mu): v = C sqrt(T/mu). Dimensional analysis cannot fix the dimensionless constant C; it has to be obtained from the exact derivation, which gives C = 1.
s: [mu] = M L^-1 and [T] = M L T^-2
T/mu = L^2 T^-2, so v is proportional to sqrt(T/mu)
The dimensionless constant C is left undetermined by the analysis (the exact derivation gives C = 1)

questions.q: A student says: 'If the frequency of a wave on a string is doubled, the speed of the wave doubles too, because v = lambda nu.' Evaluate this statement.
questions.a: The statement is incorrect. The speed on a given string under a given tension is fixed by the tension and the linear mass density, not by the frequency. When the frequency is doubled the speed stays the same and the wavelength v/nu is halved.
s: Judgement: incorrect; the speed is set by the properties of the string (T and mu), not by the frequency
With the speed unchanged, doubling nu halves the wavelength (lambda = v/nu)

questions.q: Make up a problem of your own about a transverse wave on a stretched string: choose a mass, a length, a tension and a frequency that give a whole-number speed, and work out the speed and the wavelength.
questions.a: Sample answer. A string of mass 0.4 kg and length 2.0 m is under a tension of 80 N, and a wave of frequency 50 Hz is sent along it. mu = 0.4/2.0 = 0.2 kg/m. v = sqrt(T/mu) = sqrt(80/0.2) = sqrt(400) = 20 m/s. Wavelength = v/nu = 20/50 = 0.4 m.

v = sqrt(T/mu) evaluated correctly with the chosen values
Wavelength = v/nu evaluated correctly, with units

concepts.name: Speed of a longitudinal wave: speed of sound in solids, liquids and gases
concepts.description: The speed sqrt(B/rho) of longitudinal waves in a fluid and sqrt(Y/rho) in a solid bar, why sound is faster in solids and liquids, and Newton's formula and its Laplace correction for gases.
concepts.idea: The speed of a longitudinal wave is set by an elastic modulus divided by the density; for sound in a gas the pressure changes are adiabatic, not isothermal.
concepts.rule: v = sqrt(B/rho) in a fluid, B = -dP/(dV/V); v = sqrt(Y/rho) in a solid bar. Solids and liquids are faster than gases because their B is much larger, by more than their larger density offsets. For an ideal gas an isothermal change gives B = P and Newton's formula v = sqrt(P/rho), which gives 280 m/s for air at STP, about 15% below the measured 331 m/s. Laplace showed the changes are adiabatic, P V^gamma = constant, so B = gamma P and v = sqrt(gamma P/rho); with gamma = 7/5 for air this gives 331.3 m/s. At constant temperature P/rho is unchanged by a change of pressure.
concepts.example: A gas with gamma = 1.4 at pressure 1.25 x 10^5 Pa and density 0.175 kg/m^3 gives v = sqrt(1.4 x 1.25 x 10^5/0.175) = sqrt(1.0 x 10^6) = 1000 m/s.

questions.q: A liquid has a bulk modulus of 1.96 x 10^9 Pa and a density of 1000 kg/m^3. Find the speed of sound in it and the time a sound pulse takes to travel 4.2 km through it.
questions.a: Speed v = sqrt(B/rho) = sqrt(1.96 x 10^9/1000) = sqrt(1.96 x 10^6) = 1400 m/s. Time t = distance/speed = 4200 m/(1400 m/s) = 3.0 s.
s: v = sqrt(B/rho) = 1400 m/s

questions.q: Air has a pressure of 1.0 x 10^5 Pa and a density of 1.25 kg/m^3, and gamma = 1.4. Find the speed of sound in it (to the nearest m/s) (a) from Newton's formula and (b) from Laplace's formula, and (c) say why the second is the appropriate one for sound in air.
questions.a: (a) Newton: v = sqrt(P/rho) = sqrt(1.0 x 10^5/1.25) = sqrt(80000) = 283 m/s. (b) Laplace: v = sqrt(gamma P/rho) = sqrt(1.4 x 80000) = sqrt(112000) = 335 m/s. (c) The pressure variations in a sound wave are so fast that there is no time for heat flow to keep the temperature constant; they are adiabatic, with bulk modulus gamma P instead of P, so Laplace's formula applies.
s: Newton's formula gives 283 m/s
Laplace's formula gives 335 m/s
Reason: the variations are adiabatic (B = gamma P), not isothermal (B = P)

questions.a: Only II

questions.q: Solids and liquids have higher mass densities than gases, yet sound travels faster in them. Explain this using v = sqrt(B/rho).
questions.a: In v = sqrt(B/rho) a larger density rho tends to lower the speed. But solids and liquids are much more difficult to compress than gases, so their bulk modulus B is much higher, and the increase in B is much greater than the increase in rho. Hence B/rho, and so the speed, is larger for solids and liquids.
s: Larger density alone would lower the speed, but solids and liquids have much larger B (they are hard to compress)
The increase in B is far greater than the increase in rho, so B/rho and hence the speed are larger

questions.q: For an ideal gas at constant temperature the pressure P and volume V obey V dP + P dV = 0 for a small change. Use this to show that the bulk modulus is B = P, write Newton's formula for the speed of sound, and evaluate it for a gas at pressure 9.0 x 10^4 Pa and density 1.0 kg/m^3.
questions.a: B = -dP/(dV/V). From V dP + P dV = 0, dP = -P dV/V, so -dP/(dV/V) = P and B = P. The speed v = sqrt(B/rho) then gives Newton's formula v = sqrt(P/rho). For P = 9.0 x 10^4 Pa and rho = 1.0 kg/m^3: v = sqrt(9.0 x 10^4) = 300 m/s.
s: Uses V dP + P dV = 0 in the definition of B to get B = P
Newton's formula v = sqrt(P/rho)

questions.q: A student says: 'If the pressure of air is doubled at the same temperature, sound travels faster, because the pressure P is in the numerator of v = sqrt(gamma P/rho).' Evaluate this statement.
questions.a: The statement is incorrect. For an ideal gas at constant temperature, P V = N kB T shows that doubling the pressure doubles the density rho as well, so P/rho is unchanged and the speed of sound does not change: it is independent of pressure.
s: Judgement: incorrect; the speed does not depend on pressure at constant temperature
At constant temperature the density is proportional to P, so P/rho is unchanged

questions.q: Choose a Young's modulus and a density for a hypothetical solid bar so that the speed of longitudinal waves in it comes out as a whole number, calculate that speed, and say whether sound travels faster or slower in it than in air at 20 degrees C, where the speed is 343 m/s.
questions.a: Sample answer. Take Y = 9.0 x 10^10 N/m^2 and rho = 1.0 x 10^4 kg/m^3. v = sqrt(Y/rho) = sqrt(9.0 x 10^6) = 3000 m/s. This is much greater than 343 m/s, so sound travels faster in the solid bar than in air.
s: Chooses values of Y and rho that give a whole-number speed
v = sqrt(Y/rho) evaluated correctly with units
Compares correctly with 343 m/s

concepts.name: Principle of superposition and interference of waves
concepts.description: The principle of superposition for pulses and harmonic waves, and interference of two equal harmonic waves of a given phase difference: constructive (in phase, amplitude 2a) and destructive (phase difference pi, amplitude zero).
concepts.idea: When waves overlap in a medium the net displacement is the algebraic sum of the individual displacements, and each wave moves on as though the others were absent.
concepts.rule: y(x, t) = y1 + y2 + ...; for waves y = f_i(x - vt), y = sum of the f_i. Pulses keep their identities after crossing. Two waves y1 = a sin(kx - omega t) and y2 = a sin(kx - omega t + phi) give y = 2a cos(phi/2) sin(kx - omega t + phi/2): a wave of the same omega and k, initial phase phi/2 and amplitude A(phi) = 2a cos(phi/2). phi = 0 or an integral multiple of 2 pi gives constructive interference, amplitude 2a; phi = pi gives destructive interference, zero everywhere.
concepts.example: Two waves of amplitude 1.5 cm each, in the same direction, in phase: resultant amplitude 3.0 cm. If they are made exactly out of phase (phi = pi) the resultant displacement is zero everywhere at all times.

questions.q: According to the principle of superposition, when two waves overlap in a medium the net displacement at a point is
questions.a: the algebraic sum of the displacements due to each wave
o: the algebraic sum of the displacements due to each wave

questions.a: After they have crossed, each pulse is permanently changed in shape by the overlap
o: After they have crossed, each pulse is permanently changed in shape by the overlap

The waves are exactly in phase and their amplitudes subtract out in the resultant wave

(b) Sum of all three displacements: +2.0 mm

questions.q: Two waves y1 = a sin(kx - omega t) and y2 = a sin(kx - omega t + phi) with a = 3.0 mm and phi = pi/3 travel along a string. Using sin A + sin B = 2 sin((A + B)/2) cos((A - B)/2), find the resultant wave, its amplitude (exact value and to 2 significant figures), and its initial phase angle.
questions.a: y = a sin(kx - omega t) + a sin(kx - omega t + phi) = 2a cos(phi/2) sin(kx - omega t + phi/2). With a = 3.0 mm and phi = pi/3, the amplitude is 2a cos(pi/6) = 6.0 x (sqrt(3)/2) = 3 sqrt(3) mm = 5.2 mm. The initial phase angle is phi/2 = pi/6, and the frequency and wavelength are those of each component.
s: Applies the identity to get y = 2a cos(phi/2) sin(kx - omega t + phi/2)

o: A is true, R is false

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

questions.a: By superposition y = y1 + y2 = a sin(kx - omega t) + a sin(kx - omega t + phi). The identity for sin A + sin B gives y = 2a cos(phi/2) sin(kx - omega t + phi/2). This is a harmonic wave moving in +x with the same omega and k as the components. Its amplitude is 2a cos(phi/2), a function of the phase difference phi.
s: Adds the two waves and shows the result is a wave in +x with the same omega and k (initial phase phi/2)
Amplitude = 2a cos(phi/2), depending on phi

questions.q: Two pulses of equal and opposite shape travel toward each other along a stretched string. Using the principle of superposition, describe what the string looks like (a) before the pulses meet, (b) at the instant they overlap exactly, and (c) after they have crossed.
questions.a: (a) Before they meet, the displacement of any element is just that due to the one pulse reaching it. (b) When they overlap exactly the displacements, being equal and opposite, add algebraically to zero everywhere, so the string is straight. (c) The pulses then emerge with their original shapes and keep moving, since each pulse moves as if the other were not present.
s: (a) Each pulse acts alone before the overlap
(b) Equal and opposite displacements add to zero, so the string is momentarily straight
(c) Each pulse reappears unchanged and moves on (each moves as if the other were absent)

questions.q: A student says: 'Two harmonic waves of equal amplitude a always produce a resultant of amplitude 2a, because the amplitudes add.' Evaluate this statement.
questions.a: The statement is incorrect. The resultant amplitude is 2a cos(phi/2), where phi is the phase difference. It equals 2a only when the waves are exactly in phase (phi = 0 or a multiple of 2 pi). It falls to zero when phi = pi, and takes values between 0 and 2a otherwise.
s: Judgement: incorrect; the amplitude is 2a cos(phi/2) and depends on the phase difference
2a only when exactly in phase; 0 when phi = pi, intermediate otherwise

questions.q: Choose an amplitude and a phase difference (not zero and not a multiple of pi) for two waves of the same direction, frequency and wavelength, calculate the amplitude and the initial phase angle of the resultant, and check that your amplitude lies within the possible range.
questions.a: Sample answer. Take a = 1.0 mm and phi = pi/3. The resultant amplitude is 2a cos(phi/2) = 2 x 1.0 x cos(pi/6) = sqrt(3) mm = 1.7 mm. The initial phase angle is phi/2 = pi/6. The possible amplitudes range from 0 (phi = pi) to 2a = 2.0 mm (phi = 0), and 1.7 mm lies between these limits.
s: Chooses valid values and uses A = 2a cos(phi/2) correctly
Initial phase angle phi/2 stated correctly
Checks that the amplitude lies between 0 and 2a

concepts.name: Reflection of waves and stationary waves: nodes and antinodes
concepts.description: Reflection of pulses and waves at rigid and non-rigid boundaries, and the stationary wave formed by two identical waves travelling in opposite directions, with its nodes and antinodes.
concepts.idea: A wave reflected at a boundary can combine with the incident wave to give a stationary wave in which the amplitude depends on position but the pattern does not move.
concepts.rule: At a rigid boundary the reflected wave suffers a phase change of pi (displacement zero at the boundary at all times); at a non-rigid (free) boundary there is no phase change and the net maximum displacement there is twice the amplitude. At an interface of two media part is reflected and part transmitted. Two equal waves y1 = a sin(kx - omega t), y2 = a sin(kx + omega t) give y = 2a sin kx cos omega t: each element oscillates with the same omega, the amplitude 2a sin kx varies with x. Nodes (zero amplitude) at x = n lambda/2, antinodes at x = (n + 1/2) lambda/2; consecutive nodes or antinodes are lambda/2 apart, so lambda is twice that distance.
concepts.example: A stationary wave y = 0.8 sin(6 pi x) cos(40 pi t) (SI units) has nodes where 6 pi x = n pi, i.e. at x = 0, 1/6 m, 1/3 m, ...; the first antinode is at x = 1/12 m.

(b) At the boundary the two pulses add, so the net maximum displacement is twice the amplitude of each: 2 x 3 cm = 6 cm.

Maximum displacement at the boundary is 2 x 3 = 6 cm

questions.q: A stationary wave on a string is y(x, t) = 3.0 sin(4 pi x) cos(200 pi t), with y in mm, x in m and t in s. Find (a) the amplitude of each of the two travelling waves that make it up, (b) their wavelength and the distance between successive nodes, and (c) the amplitude of the oscillation at x = 0.125 m.
questions.a: Comparing with y = 2a sin kx cos omega t: (a) 2a = 3.0 mm, so a = 1.5 mm. (b) k = 4 pi rad/m, so lambda = 2 pi/k = 0.5 m, and successive nodes are lambda/2 = 0.25 m apart. (c) At x = 0.125 m, 4 pi x = pi/2, sin(pi/2) = 1, so the amplitude is 3.0 mm (an antinode).
s: Component amplitude a = 1.5 mm
lambda = 2 pi/k = 0.5 m and node spacing 0.25 m
Amplitude at x = 0.125 m is 3.0 mm (sin(pi/2) = 1, an antinode)

questions.q: (I) At a rigid boundary a reflected pulse suffers a phase change of pi, so that the net displacement at the boundary is zero at all times. (II) At the open end of an organ pipe, treated as a non-rigid boundary, the reflected wave suffers a phase change of pi. Which is or are correct?

questions.q: Two equal waves travelling in opposite directions on a string produce a stationary wave. Explain why it is called 'stationary' by referring to the positions of the nodes and to the amplitude at a given location.
questions.a: The wave pattern is neither moving to the right nor to the left. The nodes, where sin kx = 0, are at fixed positions that do not change with time, and at each location the amplitude 2a sin kx is fixed (though different at different locations), so the pattern stays in place instead of travelling.
s: The pattern does not move left or right; the nodes stay at fixed positions
The amplitude at a given location is fixed, though it differs from one location to another

questions.q: A wave y1 = a sin(kx - omega t) travelling in +x and a wave y2 = a sin(kx + omega t) travelling in -x are superposed on a string. Using sin(A + B) + sin(A - B) = 2 sin A cos B, find the resultant displacement, find the positions of the nodes, and state the distance between two successive nodes.
questions.a: y = y1 + y2 = a[sin(kx - omega t) + sin(kx + omega t)] = 2a sin kx cos omega t. Nodes are where the amplitude 2a sin kx is zero, i.e. sin kx = 0, so kx = n pi. With k = 2 pi/lambda this gives x = n lambda/2, for n = 0, 1, 2, ... Successive nodes are therefore lambda/2 apart.
s: y = 2a sin kx cos omega t
Nodes at sin kx = 0, so x = n lambda/2
Distance between successive nodes = lambda/2

questions.q: A student says: 'In a stationary wave the nodes are just points that happen to be at rest for an instant, like every other point of the string at certain moments.' Evaluate this statement.
questions.a: The statement is incorrect. A node is a position of zero amplitude: sin kx = 0 there, so the element at a node does not move at any time. Other points pass through zero displacement together only at the instants when cos omega t = 0 and move at other times.
s: Judgement: incorrect; at a node the amplitude is zero (sin kx = 0), so it is at rest at all times

concepts.name: Normal modes of vibration: stretched strings and air columns
concepts.description: Why boundary conditions allow only certain natural frequencies, and the normal modes (harmonics) of a string fixed at both ends, an air column closed at one end and an air column open at both ends; resonance.
concepts.idea: A system with boundaries can oscillate as a stationary wave only at certain natural frequencies, the normal modes, fixed by the boundary conditions and the wave speed.
concepts.rule: String fixed at both ends (nodes at both ends): L = n lambda/2, lambda = 2L/n, nu_n = n v/(2L), n = 1, 2, 3, ...; n = 1 is the fundamental or first harmonic. Air column closed at one end (node at the closed end, antinode at the open end): L = (n + 1/2) lambda/2, nu = (n + 1/2) v/(2L), n = 0, 1, 2, ...; the fundamental is v/(4L) and only the odd harmonics 3v/(4L), 5v/(4L), ... occur. Pipe open at both ends (antinodes at both ends): nu_n = n v/(2L), all harmonics. Each normal-mode frequency is a resonant frequency: the system resonates when the external frequency is close to one of them. A vibrating string is generally a superposition of several modes.
concepts.example: A string of length 0.90 m fixed at both ends, with wave speed 180 m/s, has nu1 = 180/(2 x 0.90) = 100 Hz, and its third harmonic has frequency 300 Hz and wavelength 0.60 m.

questions.q: Explain, using the boundary conditions at the ends, why a pipe closed at one end has only odd harmonics while a pipe open at both ends has all harmonics.

concepts.name: Beats
concepts.description: The beating of two harmonic sound waves of close, unequal frequencies: the resultant s = [2a cos(omega_b t)] cos(omega_a t), the waxing and waning of intensity, and the beat frequency nu1 - nu2.
concepts.idea: Two waves of nearly equal frequency superpose to give a tone of the average frequency whose intensity waxes and wanes at the frequency difference.
concepts.rule: For s1 = a cos(omega1 t) and s2 = a cos(omega2 t), s = [2a cos(omega_b t)] cos(omega_a t) with omega_b = (omega1 - omega2)/2 and omega_a = (omega1 + omega2)/2. If |omega1 - omega2| is much smaller than omega1 and omega2, omega_a is much greater than omega_b: the tone has the average frequency and a slowly varying amplitude. Intensity is largest when cos(omega_b t) = +1 or -1, so it waxes and wanes at 2 omega_b = omega1 - omega2, and nu_beat = nu1 - nu2 (the difference). Increasing the tension of a string raises its frequency. Musicians tune until no beats are heard.
concepts.example: Forks of 128 Hz and 130 Hz sounded together give a tone of about 129 Hz whose intensity waxes and wanes 2 times per second (beat frequency 2 Hz).
